people/benedict-of-nursia/summary: Italian hermit who founded monasteries at Subiaco and Monte Cassino and wrote the Rule of St Benedict — a 'little rule for beginners' balancing prayer (opus Dei), work and study under an abbot. Through Carolingian promotion it became the norm of Western monasticism; he is patron of Europe.
people/columba/summary: Irish monk of royal lineage who founded the monastery of Iona in 563, from which he and his monks evangelised the Picts. Adomnán's Life presents him as prophet and wonder-worker; Iona's mission later reached Northumbria.
people/gregory-the-great/summary: Roman prefect turned monk, elected pope in 590 amid plague and Lombard invasion. He organised relief, sent Augustine to England, wrote the Pastoral Rule and Moralia on Job, and called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. His theology transmitted Augustine to the medieval West.
people/gregory-the-great/keyIdeas/2: Purgatory and penance in popular teaching
people/maximus-the-confessor/summary: Byzantine monk and the great synthesiser of Greek patristic theology, who opposed imperial Monothelitism by insisting that Christ has a fully human will freely united with the divine. Tried in Constantinople, his tongue and right hand were cut off and he died in exile; the council of 681 vindicated him.
people/isaac-of-nineveh/summary: Born in Beth Qatraye (Qatar), Isaac was briefly bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East before withdrawing to the mountains of Khuzistan. His ascetical homilies on humility, tears and God's boundless mercy were translated into Greek and became beloved across Orthodoxy despite his church affiliation.
people/isaac-of-nineveh/keyIdeas/0: Mercy of God for all creation
people/alopen/summary: A Church of the East missionary (fl. 635) from Persia or Syria, the first recorded Christian missionary to China. The Xi'an Stele says he arrived at Chang'an bearing scriptures and images and was welcomed by Emperor Taizong, who authorised a monastery in 638.
people/alopen/keyIdeas/0: Expression of the gospel in Chinese idiom
people/john-of-damascus/summary: Born into a Christian family serving the Umayyad caliphs at Damascus, John became a monk at Mar Saba near Jerusalem. His Fount of Knowledge systematised Greek patristic doctrine, his Three Treatises defended icons on the basis of the incarnation, and he wrote one of the earliest Christian responses to Islam.
people/timothy-i/summary: Catholicos of the Church of the East (780–823) resident in Abbasid Baghdad. He debated Christianity respectfully with Caliph al-Mahdi, translated Aristotle for the caliph, and organised metropolitan provinces from Damascus to China and Tibet, presiding over the church's widest reach.
people/charlemagne/summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor from 800, Charlemagne united much of Western Europe, forcibly converted the Saxons and sponsored the Carolingian renaissance of learning, liturgy and script. His court promoted the Filioque and the Rule of Benedict.
people/gottschalk/summary: Saxon monk given to the monastery as a child, who taught a 'double predestination' of the elect to life and the reprobate to death, drawing on Augustine. Condemned at Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849), he spent the rest of his life imprisoned at Hautvillers.
people/gottschalk/keyIdeas/1: Christ died only for the elect
people/photius/summary: Immensely learned lay scholar elevated to patriarch in 858, whose dispute with Pope Nicholas I produced the 'Photian schism'. His Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit is the classic Orthodox case against the Filioque; he sent Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. Orthodox venerate him as 'the Great'.
people/photius/keyIdeas/0: Procession of the Spirit from the Father alone
people/photius/keyIdeas/1: Equality of patriarchates against papal jurisdiction
people/john-scotus-eriugena/summary: Irish scholar at the court of Charles the Bald who translated Pseudo-Dionysius and Maximus into Latin and wrote the Periphyseon, a Neoplatonic vision of all things proceeding from and returning to God. He opposed Gottschalk; some of his views were later condemned.
people/john-scotus-eriugena/keyIdeas/2: Greek patristics in the Latin West
people/cyril-and-methodius/summary: Brothers from Thessalonica — Constantine-Cyril (c. 827–869) and Methodius (c. 815–885) — sent to Great Moravia in 863. They devised the Glagolitic alphabet and translated the Scriptures and liturgy into Slavonic, defending vernacular worship in Rome. Honoured as 'apostles to the Slavs' and patrons of Europe.
people/symeon-new-theologian/summary: Abbot of St Mamas in Constantinople whose Hymns of Divine Love and Discourses describe visions of divine light and insist that conscious experience of the Holy Spirit is the birthright of every Christian. His teaching led to exile but foreshadowed hesychasm.
people/vladimir-the-great/summary: Grand Prince of Kyiv who, after a pagan youth, chose Byzantine Christianity around 988, married the emperor's sister Anna and ordered the baptism of his people. He built the Church of the Tithes and is venerated by Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians as baptiser of Rus'.
people/vladimir-the-great/keyIdeas/1: Byzantine Orthodoxy among the East Slavs
people/anselm/summary: Italian-born abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury, a founder of scholasticism. His Proslogion offers the 'ontological argument' for God's existence ('that than which nothing greater can be conceived'), and Cur Deus Homo the satisfaction theory of atonement. He defended church liberty against English kings.
people/abelard/summary: Brilliant Paris master whose dialectical method (Sic et Non) and theology attracted crowds and controversy. After his love affair with Héloïse and castration, he became a monk; Bernard of Clairvaux secured his condemnation in 1141. He is associated with a 'moral influence' view of the atonement.
people/bernard-of-clairvaux/summary: Cistercian abbot and the dominant churchman of the twelfth century: mystic of the Song of Songs, adviser to popes, opponent of Abelard and preacher of the Second Crusade. Luther and Calvin admired his Christ-centred piety.
people/hildegard-of-bingen/summary: Benedictine abbess in the Rhineland whose visions, recorded in Scivias, were approved by Pope Eugenius III. She composed liturgical music, wrote on medicine and natural science, corresponded with emperors and popes and preached publicly. She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
people/joachim-of-fiore/summary: Calabrian abbot who read history in three ages — of the Father, the Son and the Spirit — with a coming age of the Spirit and of contemplative monks. His Trinitarian criticism of Peter Lombard was condemned in 1215, but his apocalypticism inspired Spiritual Franciscans and later millennial thought.
people/dominic/summary: Castilian canon who, after preaching to Cathars in Languedoc in poverty, founded the Order of Preachers (approved 1216) devoted to study and preaching. The Dominicans spread to universities across Europe; tradition credits him with promoting the rosary.
people/francis-of-assisi/summary: Son of a cloth merchant who renounced his wealth to live the Gospel in radical poverty, founding the Friars Minor and, with Clare, the Poor Clares. He met Sultan al-Kamil in Egypt (1219), composed the Canticle of the Creatures and reportedly received the stigmata in 1224.
people/bonaventure/summary: Franciscan theologian at Paris and minister general of his order, often called its second founder. His Journey of the Mind into God unites Augustinian illumination with Franciscan devotion; he died during the Council of Lyon (1274).
people/bonaventure/keyIdeas/0: Ascent of the mind to God
people/bonaventure/keyIdeas/1: Christ as centre of all knowledge
people/thomas-aquinas/summary: Dominican friar and master at Paris, whose Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Christian revelation. He taught that grace perfects nature, articulated transubstantiation and natural law, and offered the 'five ways' to God. Canonised in 1323, he became the Catholic Church's pre-eminent theologian.
people/thomas-aquinas/keyIdeas/3: Transubstantiation explained through substance and accidents
people/john-of-montecorvino/summary: Italian Franciscan who reached the Yuan capital Khanbaliq in 1294 after a stay in India, built churches, trained choirboys and translated the New Testament and Psalms. Named first archbishop of Khanbaliq (1307), he led the first Catholic mission in China until his death.
people/rabban-sauma/summary: A Turkic (Önggüd or Uyghur) monk of the Church of the East born near Khanbaliq, who set out on pilgrimage to Jerusalem with his disciple Markos (later Catholicos Yahballaha III). Sent by the Ilkhan Arghun as ambassador to Europe in 1287, he met the Byzantine emperor, Pope Nicholas IV and the kings of France and England.
people/rabban-sauma/keyIdeas/1: Unity of Christians East and West
people/meister-eckhart/summary: Dominican theologian and preacher whose German sermons speak of the birth of the Word in the soul and of detachment (Gelassenheit) leading into the 'ground' of God beyond all names. Some propositions were condemned in 1329, after his death; he remains a key figure of Western mysticism.
people/meister-eckhart/keyIdeas/0: Birth of God in the soul
